extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, compositors, and publishers (especially University of Chicago Press staff)
extracted.subtask_description: A typographical/style manual prescribing rules for composition, capitalization, italics, quotations, punctuation, divisions, footnotes, indexing, tabular work, and specimen types for publications of the University of Chicago Press. It is intended to guide editorial and production decisions and contains numbered rules with examples and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1. Proper nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize proper nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns (e.g., George, America, Elizabethan, French).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize verbs derived from proper names (e.g., to boycott, to pasteurize).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2. Epithets used as substitutes for proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize epithets used as substitutes for proper names or affixed to a name (e.g., the Pretender, Richard the Lion-hearted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given illustrate usage when the epithet functions in place of the name or is attached as a formal epithet.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3. Particles in French names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize particles like 'Le', 'La', 'De', 'Du' when standing without a Christian name or title preceding; do not capitalize when preceded by such name or title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Le Bossu, La Rochelle; but Rene le Bossu, Miguel de la Torre. Always capitalize 'Van' in Dutch names; never capitalize 'von' in German names (Stephen Van Rensselaer; Hugo von Martius).

rubrics_metrics.name: 4. Generic terms forming part of geographical names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize generic terms that form an organic part of geographic names (e.g., Atlantic Ocean, Mississippi River, Mount of Olives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic terms when added merely by way of description (the river Elbe, the desert of Sahara). A list of generic terms that are capitalized when forming part of names is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5. Adjectives and nouns distinguishing definite regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize adjectives and nouns used singly or together to distinguish definite regions or groups of states (e.g., Old World, Western Hemisphere, the North, Middle Western states).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not as a rule capitalize adjectives derived from such names or simple directional nouns (oriental customs, northern Europe), with noted exceptions (Northman).

rubrics_metrics.name: 6. Generic terms for political divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize terms for political divisions when they are an organic part of the name, used with 'of' as an integral name, or when used singly as an accepted designation for a specific division (e.g., Holy Roman Empire; Department of the Lakes; the Union).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize when used alone or paraphrastically (the empire, the state) except for exceptions noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7. Numbered political divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize numbered political divisions (e.g., Eleventh Congressional District, First Ward, Second Precinct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references to rule 100 for related detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8. Names of thoroughfares, parks, squares, buildings, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize proper names of streets, parks, squares, blocks, buildings, etc. (e.g., Drexel Avenue; Lincoln Park; White House).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize general designations like 'courthouse', 'post-office', 'library' except when part of the proper name or to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 9. Names of political parties, denominations, schools and adherents
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of political parties, religious denominations, philosophical/literary/artistic schools and their adherents (e.g., Republican, Catholic, Epicurean).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize these words when used in their general sense (republican form of government, socialism as an economic theory).

rubrics_metrics.name: 10. Names of monastic orders and their members
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of monastic orders and their members (e.g., Black Friars, Dominican, Jesuit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given as a direct rule without extended exceptions in this entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: 11. Proper (official) titles of organizations and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize official titles of social, religious, educational, political, commercial, and industrial organizations and institutions when used specifically (e.g., Union League Club; State University of Iowa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic terms when used to designate a class or when standing alone (young people's societies; the club); some usages where a short form is used as the name see exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12. Names of legislative, judiciary and administrative bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize such names and their branches when specifically applied (e.g., Congress, Parliament, Supreme Court of the United States, Department of the Interior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize general or incomplete designations (the legislature of the state, the council).

rubrics_metrics.name: 13. Ordinals for dynasties, sessions, regiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize ordinals used to designate Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, names of regiments, and similar connections (e.g., the Eighteenth Dynasty, Fifty-third Congress).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 100 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 14. Commonly accepted appellations for historical epochs and geological ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize widely accepted epoch names, periods in language/literature history, and geological ages (e.g., Crusades, Renaissance, Pleistocene).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word 'age' is capitalized only where necessary to avoid ambiguity (Middle Ages is capitalized; Stone age lowercase is allowed).

rubrics_metrics.name: 15. Names for important events
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of important events (e.g., Thirty Years' War, Declaration of Independence, Battle of Gettysburg).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include various wars, treaties, purchases, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 16. Political alliances and historically significant secular/ecclesiastical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize political alliances and historically significant terms that acquired designation for parties, classes, or movements (e.g., Protestant League, Holy Alliance, the Roses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 9 for relationships to parties and movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: 17. Conventions, congresses, expositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of conventions, congresses, expositions, and similar gatherings (e.g., Council of Nicaea, Chicago World's Fair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes numbered congresses and named assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: 18. Titles of specific treaties, acts, laws, and juridical documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of treaties, acts, laws, bills, and juridical documents (e.g., Treaty of Verdun, Magna Charta, Fourteenth Amendment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'the Constitution' is capitalized when referring to the U.S. Constitution standing alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: 19. Creeds and confessions of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of creeds and confessions (e.g., Apostles' Creed, Nicene Creed, Augsburg Confession).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions noted (ante-Nicene lowercased in some contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: 20. Civic and ecclesiastical feast-days
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize specific feast-days and civic holidays (e.g., Fourth of July, Thanksgiving Day, Easter, Passover).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize 'sabbath' as a generic day of rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: 21. Titles preceding the name and abbreviated academic degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of persons preceding the name and academic degrees in abbreviated form following the name; capitalize titles of honor or nobility when referring to specific persons or incumbents (e.g., Queen Victoria, Rear-Admiral Dewey, Timothy Dwight, D.D., LL.D.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize titles when following the name in general descriptive contexts (McKinley, president of the United States). See rule 49 and 25 for related exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 22. Abbreviations like Ph.D., M.P., F.R.G.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Set such abbreviated titles without spaces between letters (e.g., Ph.D., M.P.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cross-references to rules 52, 103, 106 for typographic setting; do not capitalize spelled-out phrases (doctor of philosophy).

rubrics_metrics.name: 23. One-letter abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize abbreviations consisting of one letter only, except for units of measurement and minor literary subdivisions (examples given: R.V., C., L.C.M.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 54, 55 for units and minor subdivisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 24. Names and pronouns designating the Supreme Being
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize nouns and adjectives designating the Supreme Being or the Christian Trinity and pronouns referring to them when not closely preceded/followed by a distinctive name (e.g., the Almighty, Father, Son, Holy Ghost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize derivatives such as (God's) fatherhood or (Jesus') sonship. Contextual clarity determines capitalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: 25. Words with acquired, limited, or special meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize words which have acquired a limited or special meaning in context (e.g., the Doctor's degree; a Freshman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize the common form when not used as a special designation (the doctorate).

rubrics_metrics.name: 26. Personified abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Nature' and similar terms when personified (e.g., 'Nature wields her scepter').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to mark personification in literary contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 27. 'Father' and 'Reformers' when ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Father' (church father) and 'Reformers' used of Reformation leaders when ambiguity would otherwise result (e.g., the Fathers, the Reformers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowercase forms used when specificity/ambiguity does not demand capitalization (the church reformers of the fifteenth century).

rubrics_metrics.name: 28. The word 'church' in properly cited titles and edifices
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Church' when it is part of properly cited titles of nationally organized bodies or part of a building's name (e.g., Church of Rome; Fifth Avenue Baptist Church).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize 'church' when standing alone in any general sense (the church = organized Christianity), except in exceptional rhetorical antitheses (see note).

rubrics_metrics.name: 29. Names for the Bible and other sacred books
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of sacred books and collective designations (e.g., Scriptures, Holy Writ, Koran, Vedas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize adjectives derived from such nouns (biblical, scriptural).

rubrics_metrics.name: 30. Versions of the Bible
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of Bible versions (e.g., King James's Version, Authorized Version, Revised Version, Septuagint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviations like A.V. and R.V. are recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: 31. Books and divisions of sacred books
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of books and divisions of sacred books (e.g., Old Testament, Exodus, Psalms, Gospel of Luke).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic words like 'book', 'psalm' when used in general descriptive senses (the five books of Moses). Cross-reference to rule 60 for form.

rubrics_metrics.name: 32. Biblical parables
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the names of biblical parables when cited (e.g., the parable of the Prodigal Son).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple statement of rule with example.

rubrics_metrics.name: 33. Miscellaneous biblical/ ecclesiastical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize certain miscellaneous terms associated with scripture and ecclesiastical history (e.g., Last Supper, Eucharist, the Passion, the Twelve).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided to illustrate scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: 34. First word of a sentence and of poetic lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a sentence, and in poetry the first word of each line; in Greek/Latin poetry, capitalize only the first word of a paragraph, not each verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show differences between English and classical verse capitalization practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35. First word after a colon
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word after a colon only when the colon introduces a complete passage or independent sentence (e.g., quotations, summaries) or where the colon has the weight of 'as follows' or 'namely'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize when the quotation is closely connected to the preceding clause or when the colon introduces a dependent explanatory phrase; examples illustrate both allowed and disallowed uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: 36. First word in sections of enumeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally capitalize the first word in enumerated sections if any link contains two or more distinct clauses separated by semicolon, colon, or period, unless all are dependent on the preceding term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show when each enumerated item begins with a capital and when not, depending on internal punctuation and dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37. Nouns followed by a numeral
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize nouns followed by a numeral indicating order in a sequence (e.g., Room 16, Act I, Vol. I, Book II).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize minor subdivisions like 'sec. 4', 'scene i', 'chap. 2 (ii)'; see cross-references to no./37 guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 38. First word of a cited speech or thought in direct discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a cited speech or thought in direct discourse, whether preceded by a colon or comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show quotations that begin with a capitalized first word and variations in punctuation leading into quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 39. Resolutions wording: 'WHEREAS' and 'Resolved'
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions, capitalize the first words following 'WHEREAS' and 'Resolved' (e.g., WHEREAS, It has pleased God... Resolved, That...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal usage illustrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: 40. Exclamations 'O' and 'Oh'
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the exclamations 'O' and 'Oh' (e.g., 'O Lord!', 'Oh, that I were home again!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule points to see also rule 117 for related punctuation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 41. Principal words in English titles of publications and headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize all principal words (nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs, verbs, first and last words) in English titles of publications and divisions, subjects of lectures, and certain types of heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes about variation: Botanical Gazette prefers only first words and proper names; cap-and-small-cap and italic center-heads are generally to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 42. Capitalization in foreign titles
rubrics_metrics.description: In foreign titles, capitalize according to the language's conventions: (a) Latin: proper nouns and adjectives derived from them; (b) French/Italian/Spanish/Scandinavian: capitalize first word and proper nouns but not derived adjectives; (c) German/Danish: capitalize all nouns but not adjectives (except German adjectives from persons); (d) Dutch: capitalize all nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given for each language illustrate the respective conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 43. Definite article in newspaper and magazine titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not, as a rule, treat the definite article as part of the title when mentioning newspapers and magazines (e.g., the Chicago Tribune, the School Review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation for typical bibliographic usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: 44. Titles of ancient manuscripts (MS, MSS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of ancient manuscripts (singular MS; plural MSS) when cited (e.g., Codex Bemensis, Cod. Canonicianus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rule 60 for related treatment of manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 45. Capitalization in hyphenated titles
rubrics_metrics.description: In titles with main words capitalized, capitalize all nouns forming parts of hyphenated compounds (e.g., 'Twentieth-Century Progress').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize hyphenated components when they are other than nouns (e.g., Fifty-first Street).

rubrics_metrics.name: 46. Scientific (Latin) names in natural sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize scientific Latin names of divisions, orders, families, and genera; do not capitalize their English derivatives (e.g., Cotylosauria but cotylosaurs; Felidae but felids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Species names are capitalized if derived from persons or from generic names in botanical and zoological contexts, but in geological and medical matter species names are never capitalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: 47. Names and epithets of peoples, races, tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes (e.g., Kafir, Negro, Makassar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule lists examples; modern sensibilities about terms are outside the historical text.

rubrics_metrics.name: 48. Astronomical names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of bodies in the solar system (except 'sun', 'earth', 'moon', 'stars') when used in astronomical work (e.g., the Milky Way, Saturn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions noted for common celestial nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: 49. University of Chicago internal divisions and titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize divisions, departments, officers, and courses of the University of Chicago in official work dealing with administration or curricula (e.g., the School of Education, the Department of Anthropology, the President).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowercase forms are used in general references (the division, the department, the faculty) except where official or to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 50. Use of capitals and small capitals for letterhead elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Set names of town and state in the dateline, salutatory phrase, and signatures in capitals and small capitals with specified alignment and indentation conventions (e.g., CHICAGO, ILL., MY DEAR MR. SMITH:).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include recommended alignment, indentation, and type size conventions for letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: 51. Capitalization in formal documents: 'WHEREAS', 'NOTE', 'SECTION'
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize specific words in formal documents: 'WHEREAS' in resolutions, 'NOTE' in notes followed by period and dash, 'SECTION' introducing constitution/by-law paragraphs followed by a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usual practice is to abbreviate 'SECTION' after its first use (SECTION i. ... SEC. 2.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 52. Set in small capitals: A.M., P.M., B.C., A.D.
rubrics_metrics.description: Set A.M., P.M., B.C., and A.D. in small capitals without spaces between letters (e.g., 11:30 A.M.; 53 B.C.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references to rules 22, 103, 106 for related typographic conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 53. Use small initial letter for commonized proper nouns and derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lowercase initial for words of common usage originally proper names and their derivatives where origin is obscured (e.g., utopia, bohemian, boycott, italicize).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This covers verbs derived from proper names and other generalized forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: 54. Lowercase minor literary subdivisions in literary references
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lowercase for minor subdivisions and their abbreviations in literary references (chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note; chap., sec., p., art., vs., l., n.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rules 37 and no. for numeral/subdivision usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: 55. Lowercase units of measurement abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lowercase abbreviations for units of measurement (h.=hour, min.=minute, sec.=second, lb.=pound, oz.=ounce, yd.=yard, ft.=foot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives standard abbreviations to be used in text and tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: 56. Italic side-heads: capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In italic side-heads, capitalize only the first word and proper names; set remaining words in lowercase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 172 and 280 for additional guidance on side-heads and tabular headings.

rubrics_metrics.name: 57. First word of a quotation connected to preceding text
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a lowercase initial for the first word of a quotation that is immediately connected with what precedes (even if that word begins a sentence in the original), unless it begins a sentence/paragraph in reduced type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See illustrations and exceptions in rules 35 and 131.

rubrics_metrics.name: 58. Italicize words for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases to which emphasis or importance is to be lent (e.g., 'This was, however, not the case').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for rhetorical emphasis in prose; examples illustrate contrastive emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: 59. Italicize foreign words and brief foreign passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize foreign words or phrases inserted into English text and not incorporated into English; also italicize single sentences or brief passages in a foreign language not long enough to warrant reduced type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or names of foreign institutions/places used as regular names (Pere Lagrange; Champs Elysees). Do not italicize words that have become anglicized even if retaining accents.
